How to Make the Gradient Mapping Small for Constrained Stochastic Min-Max Problems and Beyond

Ahmet Alacaoglu Note: Department of Mathematics, University of British Columbia, ahmet.alacaoglu@ubc.ca
Abstract

We study the stochastic first-order oracle complexity for constrained or regularized convex-concave min-max optimization and stochastic monotone variational inequalities. We focus on the case when suboptimality is measured in terms of the gradient mapping, also known as, forward-backward or natural residual, an optimality notion that generalizes the gradient norm for unconstrained problems. In this setting, under standard unbiased oracle access with now-standard variance assumptions, the best-known complexity for making the norm of the gradient mapping less than ε\varepsilon is O~​(ε−4)\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-4}), compared to the near-optimal O~​(ε−2)\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}) that is established in the unconstrained case. We bridge this gap to improve the gradient mapping complexity for constrained convex-concave min-max problems to O~​(ε−2)\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}). We then extend to prove the same complexity for problems without the bounded variance, by using the Blum-Gladyshev assumption.

1 Introduction

We study algorithms to solve the standard template of constrained convex-concave min-max optimization,

min𝐮∈U⁡max𝐯∈V⁡f⁡(𝐮,𝐯),\min_{\mathbf{u}\in U}\max_{\mathbf{v}\in V}f(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}), (1.1)

where f⁡(⋅,𝐯)f(\cdot,\mathbf{v}) is convex, f⁡(𝐮,⋅)f(\mathbf{u},\cdot) is concave, the gradients ∇𝐮f​(𝐮,𝐯),∇𝐯f​(𝐮,𝐯)\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}f(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}),\nabla_{\mathbf{v}}f(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}) are Lipschitz continuous, and U⊆ℝn,V⊆ℝmU\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n},V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m} are closed convex sets admitting efficient projection operators.

Two canonical examples of this template come from cases where the coupling between 𝐮\mathbf{u} and 𝐯\mathbf{v} is bilinear, such as matrix games

min𝐮∈Δn⁡max𝐯∈Δm​⟨A​𝐮,𝐯⟩,\min_{\mathbf{u}\in\Delta_{n}}\max_{\mathbf{v}\in\Delta_{m}}\langle A\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\rangle, (1.2)

where Δn\Delta_{n} denotes the probability simplex, that is, Δn={𝐮∈ℝ+n:∑i=1nui=1}\Delta_{n}=\{\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}\colon\sum_{i=1}^{n}u_{i}=1\}.

The second common example is linearly constrained optimization

min𝐮∈ℝn⁡f⁡(𝐮):A​𝐮≤𝐛,\min_{\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}f(\mathbf{u}):A\mathbf{u}\leq\mathbf{b},

for a proper, convex and closed function f:ℝn→(−∞,∞]f\colon\mathbb{R}^{n}\to(-\infty,\infty]. Solving this problem efficiently is generally done by utilizing convex duality to convert to a min-max problem given as

min𝐮∈ℝn⁡max𝐯≥0⁡f⁡(𝐮)+⟨A​𝐮−𝐛,𝐯⟩.\min_{\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\max_{\mathbf{v}\geq 0}f(\mathbf{u})+\langle A\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{b},\mathbf{v}\rangle. (1.3)

Strictly speaking, this problem does not fit the template (1.1) due to potential nonsmoothness in ff. However, our focus on (1.1) in this section is purely for a simple presentation. In the sequel, we develop our results for the more general problem of variational inequalities to cover this example, see (VI) for a precise problem statement.

We will focus on a setting where we do not have access to gradients ∇𝐮f​(𝐮,𝐯)\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}f(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}) and ∇𝐯f​(𝐮,𝐯)\nabla_{\mathbf{v}}f(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}), but to their unbiased estimators such that

𝔼⁡[∇𝐮fξ​(𝐮,𝐯)]=∇𝐮f​(𝐮,𝐯),\mathbb{E}[\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}f_{\xi}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})]=\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}f(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}),

where ξ\xi is sampled from an unknown distribution PP, where we can have f⁡(𝐮,𝐯)=𝔼ξ∼P​[fξ​(𝐮,𝐯)]f(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim P}[f_{\xi}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})]. At every iteration of our algorithm, we will assume that we receive i.i.d. samples ξ∼P\xi\sim P.

More concretely, for (1.2) or (1.3), these stochastic oracles may correspond to randomly sampling rows or columns from the matrix AA, whereas the full-gradients require accessing the matrix AA at every iteration. A concrete example is given at the end of Section 1.1.

Two optimality notions.

Arguably, the most widely used optimality notion for min-max problems is the primal-dual gap

Gap⁡(𝐮¯,𝐯¯)=max𝐮∈U,𝐯∈V⁡f⁡(𝐮¯,𝐯)−f⁡(𝐮,𝐯¯).\mathrm{Gap}(\bar{\mathbf{u}},\bar{\mathbf{v}})=\max_{\mathbf{u}\in U,\mathbf{v}\in V}f(\bar{\mathbf{u}},\mathbf{v})-f(\mathbf{u},\bar{\mathbf{v}}).

This is well-suited to problems such as matrix games in (1.2), however, when the sets U,VU,V are unbounded, such as the case of linearly constrained optimization in (1.3), this notion runs into problems. In particular, this quantity may be infinite at test points 𝐮¯,𝐯¯\bar{\mathbf{u}},\bar{\mathbf{v}} that are not optimal.

This well-known drawback gave rise to the restricted primal-dual gap function (Nes, 09) that takes the maximum over a compact set that needs to satisfy certain requirements. That is, this set needs to contain a solution and the iterates of the algorithm, see (Nes, 09, Lemma 4). This approach can be compatible in the deterministic case when the boundedness of the iterates can be shown for standard methods.

For stochastic algorithms, boundedness of the iterates does not generally hold, causing difficulty in identifying a compact set to define the restricted gap function á la Nes (09). Moreover, the restricted gap is generally taken over sets that generally depend on the solution, making it difficult to compute in general.

Despite its incompatibility with unbounded domains and stochastic problems, this notion is widely used because the standard convergence analyses for algorithms, such as extragradient (Kor, 76) or forward-backward-forward (FBF) methods (Tse, 00), give a rate result on the gap as a byproduct. As a result, optimal methods for reducing the gap is well-established for both deterministic and stochastic problems (Nem, 04; NJLS, 09).

Perhaps even a more natural way of measuring suboptimality for unbounded problems is the gradient mapping norm (Nes, 13, Section 2), which generalizes the gradient norm for unconstrained problems

‖𝒢η,f​(𝐱,𝐲)‖2=1η2​(‖𝐱−projU⁡(𝐱−η​∇𝐱f​(𝐱,𝐲))‖2+‖𝐲−projV⁡(𝐲+η​∇𝐲f​(𝐱,𝐲))‖2),\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta,f}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\|^{2}=\frac{1}{\eta^{2}}\left(\|\mathbf{x}-\operatorname{proj}_{U}(\mathbf{x}-\eta\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}f(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}))\|^{2}+\|\mathbf{y}-\operatorname{proj}_{V}(\mathbf{y}+\eta\nabla_{\mathbf{y}}f(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}))\|^{2}\right), (1.4)

where projC\operatorname{proj}_{C} denotes the Euclidean projection on CC. While this notion is widely used for nonconvex problems, optimal complexity results for making this quantity small, even for convex minimization problems is relatively recent, see Nes (12) for deterministic and AZ (18) for stochastic optimization.

Clearly, this reduces to the gradient norm when (U,V)=(ℝn,ℝm)(U,V)=(\mathbb{R}^{n},\mathbb{R}^{m}) since

𝒢η,f​(𝐱,𝐲)=(∇𝐱f​(𝐱,𝐲)−∇𝐲f​(𝐱,𝐲)).\mathcal{G}_{\eta,f}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\binom{\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}f(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})}{-\nabla_{\mathbf{y}}f(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})}.

Optimal methods for reducing the gradient – or gradient mapping – norm for deterministic convex-concave min-max problems is established relatively recently as well, see Dia (20); Kim (21); YR (21); KG (22). An optimal method for unconstrained and stochastic min-max problems is proposed in CL (24) who showed the complexity O~​(ε−2)\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}) for making the gradient norm less than ε\varepsilon with matching lower bounds.

Yet, the best-known complexity for constrained min-max problems, which are of interest in terms of many applications – such as matrix games (1.2), linearly constrained optimization (1.3), and distributionally robust optimization (ND, 16, Eq. (1)) – remained at O~​(ε−4)\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-4}) – with the exception of TDNT (26) that improved this to O~(ε−10/3)\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-10/3}) under stronger assumptions on the stochastic oracle, see Table 1. The goal of this work is to improve this complexity to one that is optimal in terms of ε\varepsilon dependence. This discussion is summarized in Table 2 where we highlighted the main setting we focus on.

Generalized problems.

For a simpler notation and a slight generalization, we will consider the problem of variational inequalities where the goal is to

find ​𝐱⋆​ such that ​⟨F⁡(𝐱⋆),𝐱−𝐱⋆⟩≥r⁡(𝐱⋆)−r⁡(𝐱)​ for any ​𝐱∈ℝd,\text{find~}\mathbf{x}^{\star}\text{~such that~}\langle F(\mathbf{x}^{\star}),\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\star}\rangle\geq r(\mathbf{x}^{\star})-r(\mathbf{x})\text{~for any~}\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, (VI)

with a proper, convex and closed r:ℝd→(−∞,∞]r\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to(-\infty,\infty] and a monotone operator11 1 Introduced in Section 1.1. F:ℝd→ℝdF\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}. Mapping (1.1) to this problem is done by setting

𝐱=(𝐮𝐯),F⁡(𝐱)=(∇𝐮f​(𝐮,𝐯)−∇𝐯f​(𝐮,𝐯)),r⁡(𝐱)=δU​(𝐮)+δV​(𝐯),\mathbf{x}=\binom{\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{v}},~~~F(\mathbf{x})=\binom{\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}f(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})}{-\nabla_{\mathbf{v}}f(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})},~~~r(\mathbf{x})=\delta_{U}(\mathbf{u})+\delta_{V}(\mathbf{v}), (1.5)

where δC​(𝐱)\delta_{C}(\mathbf{x}) denotes the indicator function, that is 00 when 𝐱∈C\mathbf{x}\in C and ∞\infty otherwise.

We will often use the equivalent form written as a monotone inclusion problem where the goal is to

find ​𝐱⋆​ such that ​0∈H⁡(𝐱⋆):=(F+∂r)​(𝐱⋆).\text{find~}\mathbf{x}^{\star}\text{~such that~}0\in H(\mathbf{x}^{\star}):=(F+\partial r)(\mathbf{x}^{\star}). (MI)

We focus on this specific monotone inclusion for presentation purposes, but by changing Algorithm 1 to a method based on FBF (Tse, 00) or forward-reflected-backward method (MT, 20), our analysis can be extended to solve general monotone inclusion where ∂r\partial r is replaced by a maximally monotone operator. We skip this extension for keeping our notation simpler.

By overloading the terminology for simplicity, we shall now write the gradient mapping as

𝒢η,H​(𝐱)=1η​(𝐱−proxη​r⁡(𝐱−η​F​(𝐱))),\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{\eta}\left(\mathbf{x}-\prox_{\eta r}(\mathbf{x}-\eta F(\mathbf{x}))\right),

which is equivalent to (1.4) with the setting (1.5). We emphasize that FF does not need to be the gradient of a function, and we merely use this notation to keep the link with min-max optimization (1.1) transparent. This notion is also referred to as forward-backward residual or natural residual (in the specific case when rr is an indicator function), see (FP, 03, Section 10.3).

Our goal in the sequel is to find an approximate solution to (MI) by making the residual small. This result directly covers making the gradient mapping small for convex-concave and constrained min-max problems by the mapping (1.5).

Complexity.

Given the problem (VI) introduced above, we measure complexity in terms of the number of calls to the unbiased stochastic oracles FξF_{\xi} such that

𝔼⁡[Fξ​(𝐱)]=F⁡(𝐱)\mathbb{E}[F_{\xi}(\mathbf{x})]=F(\mathbf{x})

and to the proximal operator of rr —which reduces to the number of calls to stochastic gradients and projections on U,VU,V in the case of min-max problems (1.1)— to get a certain optimality notion less than ε\varepsilon.

There exists now a large body of works that analyze methods such as stochastic extragradient with optimal complexity for reducing the gap. That is, it is well-known how to get

𝔼⁡[Gap⁡(𝐱¯,𝐲¯)]≤ε, with complexity ​O​(ε−2).\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Gap}(\bar{\mathbf{x}},\bar{\mathbf{y}})]\leq\varepsilon,\text{~with complexity~}O(\varepsilon^{-2}).

We refer to NJLS (09); JNT (11); KLL (22); Zha (22); LL (26) for representative examples.

Moreover, when r≡0r\equiv 0, that is, we have a root finding problem, CL (24) established the oracle complexity

O~​(ε−2)​ for making ​𝔼​‖F⁡(𝐱)‖≤ε,\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})\text{~for making~}\mathbb{E}\|F(\mathbf{x})\|\leq\varepsilon,

which is optimal. The authors assumed that the unbiased oracle has bounded variance upper bounded by σ2\sigma^{2} and designed an algorithm that sets its parameters by using σ2\sigma^{2} and ‖𝐱0−𝐱⋆‖2\|\mathbf{x}_{0}-\mathbf{x}^{\star}\|^{2}, the initial distance of their initial point to a solution. For unconstrained problems, with stronger assumptions such as sharpness, CSGD (22) also obtained a similar complexity, yet for unconstrained and merely monotone problems, the complexity in this work deteriorated to O~​(ε−3)\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-3}).

For constrained problems, the best-known complexity for the gradient mapping under our assumptions is

O⁡(ε−4)​ for making ​𝔼​‖𝒢η,H​(𝐱)‖≤ε,O(\varepsilon^{-4})\text{~for making~}\mathbb{E}\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H}(\mathbf{x})\|\leq\varepsilon,

which is suboptimal. This complexity remained as the best-known on a large body of literature for constrained or regularized min-max problems (IJOT, 17; BMSV, 21; AMW, 25; LK, 21; PFL+, 23; Böh, 23; DDJ, 21; TDNT, 25). Even though some of these works relied on some relaxations of convex-concavity, none of the analyses in those works gave rise to a better complexity for convex-concave problems. The aim of this work is to improve this complexity for problems satisfying the Blum-Gladyshev variance and without requiring parameters depending on initial distance to solution or variance upper bounds.

A recent work by TDNT (26) obtained a complexity of O~(ε−10/3)\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-10/3}) for constrained problems by using variance reduction. Different from our work, they required a multi-point oracle that requires querying the stochastic oracle at the same seed for different points, the mean-square Lipschitzness assumption (which is stronger than mere Lipschitzness of FF) and bounded variance.

1.1 Notation and Preliminaries

Given the history of random vectors ξ0,ξ0.5,…,ξk\xi_{0},\xi_{0.5},\dots,\xi_{k}, we denote the expectation conditioned on the generated σ\sigma-algebra as 𝔼k[⋅]=𝔼[⋅|σ(ξ0,ξ0.5,…,ξk)]\mathbb{E}_{k}[\cdot]=\mathbb{E}[\cdot~|~\sigma(\xi_{0},\xi_{0.5},\dots,\xi_{k})]. For a vector 𝐱\mathbf{x}, the notation xix_{i} refers to its ii-th coordinate.

In this paper, we always consider a regularizer r:ℝd→(−∞,∞]r\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to(-\infty,\infty] that is convex, proper and closed. Its subdifferential set is denoted as ∂r\partial r. We define the proximal operator of rr as

proxr⁡(𝐱)=arg⁡min𝐲⁡r⁡(𝐲)+12​‖𝐱−𝐲‖2,\prox_{r}(\mathbf{x})=\arg\min_{\mathbf{y}}r(\mathbf{y})+\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\|^{2}, (1.6)

from which we can derive the prox-inequality, by using the optimality condition of (1.6),

𝐲=proxr⁡(𝐱)⇔⟨𝐲−𝐱,𝐮−𝐲⟩≥r⁡(𝐲)−r⁡(𝐮)​∀𝐮∈ℝd.\mathbf{y}=\prox_{r}(\mathbf{x})\iff\langle\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x},\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{y}\rangle\geq r(\mathbf{y})-r(\mathbf{u})~~~\forall\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. (1.7)

When r⁡(𝐱)=δC​(𝐱)={0, if ​𝐱∈C,∞, if ​𝐱∉C,r(\mathbf{x})=\delta_{C}(\mathbf{x})=\begin{cases}0,\text{~if~}\mathbf{x}\in C,\\ \infty,\text{~if~}\mathbf{x}\not\in C,\end{cases} this reduces to the projection operator

projC⁡(𝐱)=arg⁡min𝐲∈C​12​‖𝐱−𝐲‖2.\operatorname{proj}_{C}(\mathbf{x})=\arg\min_{\mathbf{y}\in C}\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\|^{2}.

We say that an operator F:ℝd→ℝdF\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} is μ\mu-strongly monotone, when

⟨F⁡(𝐱)−F⁡(𝐲),𝐱−𝐲⟩≥μ​‖𝐱−𝐲‖2,\langle F(\mathbf{x})-F(\mathbf{y}),\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\rangle\geq\mu\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\|^{2},

and monotone when this inequality holds with μ=0\mu=0.

The operator FF is LFL_{F}-Lipschitz when

‖F⁡(𝐱)−F⁡(𝐲)‖≤LF​‖𝐱−𝐲‖.\|F(\mathbf{x})-F(\mathbf{y})\|\leq L_{F}\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\|.

Recalling our mapping F=(∇𝐮f​(𝐮,𝐯)−∇𝐯f​(𝐮,𝐯))F=\binom{\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}f(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})}{-\nabla_{\mathbf{v}}f(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})} for a convex-concave ff, this corresponds to Lipschitzness of the gradients of ∇𝐮f​(𝐮,𝐯),∇𝐯f​(𝐮,𝐯)\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}f(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}),\nabla_{\mathbf{v}}f(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}).

Assumption 1.

For problem (MI), let FF be monotone and LFL_{F}-Lipschitz. Assume that rr is proper, convex, closed. There exists 𝐱⋆\mathbf{x}^{\star} such that 0∈(F+∂r)​(𝐱⋆)0\in(F+\partial r)(\mathbf{x}^{\star}). We have access to an unbiased estimator of FF such that 𝔼⁡[Fξ​(𝐱)]=F⁡(𝐱)\mathbb{E}[F_{\xi}(\mathbf{x})]=F(\mathbf{x}).

In view of the mapping (1.5), Assumption 1 is satisfied when f⁡(𝐮,𝐯)f(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}) is convex-concave (implies that FF is monotone), the gradients ∇𝐮f​(𝐮,𝐯)\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}f(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}) and ∇𝐯f​(𝐮,𝐯)\nabla_{\mathbf{v}}f(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}) are Lipschitz continuous (implies that FF is Lipschitz) and U,VU,V are convex closed sets (implies the requirements on rr).

We now present the Blum-Gladyshev (BG) assumption from Gla (65); Blu (54) that is studied for minimization and min-max problems recently.

Assumption 2 (Blum-Gladyshev variance).

Let the unbiased estimator of FF satisfy

𝔼​‖Fξ​(𝐱)−F⁡(𝐱)‖2≤B2​‖𝐱−𝐳̊‖2+G2,\mathbb{E}\|F_{\xi}(\mathbf{x})-F(\mathbf{x})\|^{2}\leq B^{2}\|\mathbf{x}-\mathring{\mathbf{z}}\|^{2}+G^{2},

where 𝐳̊\mathring{\mathbf{z}} is a fixed initial point. In view of Assumption 1, denote L^F=LF+B\widehat{L}_{F}=L_{F}+B.

The reason for selecting 𝐳̊\mathring{\mathbf{z}} as the center in the assumption is for convenience. One can change it to any other fixed center point, by absorbing the difference in the constant GG and slightly changing BB.

We also define the initial distance to a solution as (see (MI))

D⋆=‖𝐳̊−𝐱⋆‖.D_{\star}=\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{x}^{\star}\|. (1.8)

Let us first remark that this is a generalization of the commonly used bounded variance assumption that is used in AZ (18); CL (24). If B=0B=0 in Assumption 2, this would correspond to assuming a bounded variance.

In the sequel, we require the knowledge of BB, but not GG for setting algorithmic parameters. As we explain now, BB is often connected to the Lipschitz constant and hence its knowledge should not be too restrictive in many cases.

Let us observe that a sufficient condition for the BG assumption is when we have F⁡(𝐱)=𝔼⁡[Fξ∼P​(𝐱)]F(\mathbf{x})=\mathbb{E}[F_{\xi\sim P}(\mathbf{x})] and Fξ​(𝐱)F_{\xi}(\mathbf{x}) is mean-square Lipschitz, that is,

𝔼​‖Fξ​(𝐱)−Fξ​(𝐲)‖2≤Lexp2​‖𝐱−𝐲‖2,\mathbb{E}\|F_{\xi}(\mathbf{x})-F_{\xi}(\mathbf{y})\|^{2}\leq L_{\exp}^{2}\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\|^{2},

and 𝔼​‖Fξ​(𝐱⋆)−F⁡(𝐱⋆)‖2≤σ⋆2\mathbb{E}\|F_{\xi}(\mathbf{x}^{\star})-F(\mathbf{x}^{\star})\|^{2}\leq\sigma_{\star}^{2}. This is sufficient because of the chain of inequalities

𝔼​‖Fξ​(𝐱)−F⁡(𝐱)‖2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|F_{\xi}(\mathbf{x})-F(\mathbf{x})\|^{2} ≤2​𝔼​‖Fξ​(𝐱)−F⁡(𝐱)−Fξ​(𝐱⋆)+F⁡(𝐱⋆)‖2+2​𝔼​‖Fξ​(𝐱⋆)−F⁡(𝐱⋆)‖2\displaystyle\leq 2\mathbb{E}\|F_{\xi}(\mathbf{x})-F(\mathbf{x})-F_{\xi}(\mathbf{x}^{\star})+F(\mathbf{x}^{\star})\|^{2}+2\mathbb{E}\|F_{\xi}(\mathbf{x}^{\star})-F(\mathbf{x}^{\star})\|^{2}
≤2​𝔼​‖Fξ​(𝐱)−Fξ​(𝐱⋆)‖2+2​𝔼​‖Fξ​(𝐱⋆)−F⁡(𝐱⋆)‖2\displaystyle\leq 2\mathbb{E}\|F_{\xi}(\mathbf{x})-F_{\xi}(\mathbf{x}^{\star})\|^{2}+2\mathbb{E}\|F_{\xi}(\mathbf{x}^{\star})-F(\mathbf{x}^{\star})\|^{2}
≤2​Lexp2​‖𝐱−𝐱⋆‖2+2​σ⋆2\displaystyle\leq 2L_{\exp}^{2}\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{\star}\|^{2}+2\sigma_{\star}^{2}
≤4​Lexp2⏟B2​‖𝐱−𝐳̊‖2+4​Lexp2​‖𝐳̊−𝐱⋆‖2+2​σ⋆2⏟G2,\displaystyle\leq\underbrace{4L_{\exp}^{2}}_{B^{2}}\|\mathbf{x}-\mathring{\mathbf{z}}\|^{2}+\underbrace{4L_{\exp}^{2}\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{x}^{\star}\|^{2}+2\sigma_{\star}^{2}}_{G^{2}},

where the first and last steps are by Young’s inequality, the second step is using 𝔼⁡[Fξ​(𝐱)−Fξ​(𝐱⋆)]=F⁡(𝐱)−F⁡(𝐱⋆)\mathbb{E}[F_{\xi}(\mathbf{x})-F_{\xi}(\mathbf{x}^{\star})]=F(\mathbf{x})-F(\mathbf{x}^{\star}) – along with the inequality 𝔼​‖X−𝔼​X‖2≤𝔼​‖X‖2\mathbb{E}\|X-\mathbb{E}X\|^{2}\leq\mathbb{E}\|X\|^{2} for random vectors XX. This proves that, for example, (MKS+, 20, Assumptions 2, 4) implies Assumption 2.

A more concrete example is the bilinearly coupled min-max problem where a common oracle is by sampling row-column pairs from matrix A∈ℝm×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}:

Fξ(𝐱)=(mAj:vj−nA:iui),F_{\xi}(\mathbf{x})=\binom{mA_{j:}v_{j}}{-nA_{:i}u_{i}},

where ξ=(i,j)\xi=(i,j) are selected uniformly at random, A:iA_{:i} is ii-th column of AA and Aj:A_{j:} is jj-th row of AA.

Then, the variance 𝔼i,j‖(mAj:vj−nA:iui)−(A⊤​v−A​𝐮)‖2\mathbb{E}_{i,j}\left\|\binom{mA_{j:}v_{j}}{-nA_{:i}u_{i}}-\binom{A^{\top}v}{-A\mathbf{u}}\right\|^{2} will not be bounded in general, unless 𝐮,𝐯\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v} live on compact sets – an unrealistic assumption in general, preventing applying the results of the form CL (24) even for unconstrained problems. Yet, the variance will scale quadratically in the norm of 𝐱=(𝐮𝐯)\mathbf{x}=\binom{\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{v}}, satisfying the BG assumption. This example can be generalized to solve problems with other affine operators and stochastic oracles.

Byproducts of our analysis also include optimal complexity guarantees for the gradient mapping norm for strongly convex-strongly concave problems. We also design algorithms not requiring difficult-to-compute constants such as the initial distance to solution, that is, ‖𝐳̊−𝐱⋆‖2\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{x}^{\star}\|^{2}, required in (CL, 24), or a global variance upper bound, required in the work (CL, 24).

2 Algorithm & Statement of Main Results

The main algorithmic construction will be based on a key idea from AZ (18) who had focused on the same goal for composite convex optimization: recursive regularization. Indeed, CL (24) had also considered extension of AZ (18) to the min-max case. However, their extension came with three main drawbacks that we will address: (1) their analysis was limited to the unconstrained problem, (2) their analysis introduced a requirement for knowing the global variance upper bound and initial distance to optimum ‖𝐳̊−𝐱⋆‖2\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{x}^{\star}\|^{2}, (3) they inherited the drawback from AZ (18) and required a globally bounded variance. We will go around these limitations by using the BG variance assumption and anchoring, proposed for a similar purpose in NO (24) for proving a complexity result for the primal-dual gap.

Recursive regularization – Algorithm 3.

In our setting, this corresponds to solving strongly monotone inclusion problems with an increasing amount of added strong monotonicity. In particular, this algorithm will give us an approximate solution for the problem

find ​𝐳0⋆​ such that ​0∈Hμ​(𝐳0⋆):=Fμ​(𝐳0⋆)+∂r⁡(𝐳0⋆),\text{find~}\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{0}\text{~such that~}0\in H^{\mu}(\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{0}):=F^{\mu}(\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star})+\partial r(\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{0}), (2.1)

where

F0​(𝐳):=Fμ​(𝐳)={F⁡(𝐳)​ if ​F​ is ​μ​-strongly monotone,F⁡(𝐳)+μ⁡(𝐳−𝐳̊)​ for some ​μ>0​ if ​F​ is monotone.F^{0}(\mathbf{z}):=F^{\mu}(\mathbf{z})=\begin{cases}F(\mathbf{z})\text{~if~}F\text{~is~}\mu\text{-strongly monotone,}\\ F(\mathbf{z})+\mu(\mathbf{z}-\mathring{\mathbf{z}})\text{~for some~}\mu>0\text{~if~}F\text{~is monotone.}\end{cases} (2.2)

This setting ensures that FμF^{\mu} is μ\mu-strongly monotone for some μ>0\mu>0, even if FF is only monotone.

Then, each step s≥1s\geq 1 of Algorithm 3 solves approximately the subproblem:

 find ​𝐳s−1⋆​ such that ​0∈(Fs−1+∂r)​(𝐳s−1⋆),\displaystyle\text{~find~}\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}\text{~such that~}0\in(F^{s-1}+\partial r)(\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}), (2.3)
 where Fs−1(𝐳)=Fs−2(𝐳)+μs−1(𝐳−𝐳s−1)=Fμ(𝐳)+∑i=1s−1μi(𝐳−𝐳i), if s≥2,\displaystyle\text{~where~}F^{s-1}(\mathbf{z})=F^{s-2}(\mathbf{z})+\mu_{s-1}(\mathbf{z}-\mathbf{z}_{s-1})=F^{\mu}(\mathbf{z})+\sum_{i=1}^{s-1}\mu_{i}(\mathbf{z}-\mathbf{z}_{i}),\text{~if~}s\geq 2,

and for s=1s=1, we have that F0F^{0} is as defined in (2.2) and 𝐳0⋆\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star} is defined in (2.1).

That is, at iteration ss, we form an auxiliary problem which is centered at current iterate 𝐳s−1\mathbf{z}_{s-1} and then use a strongly monotone subsolver in Algorithm 2 to solve this problem. The amount of strong monotonicity added is increasing exponentially fast, that is μs=2s​μ\mu_{s}=2^{s}\mu where μ\mu is the initial strong monotonicity of F0=FμF^{0}=F^{\mu} defined in (2.2).

Our main aim is to solve a monotone problem, but similar to AZ (18), the approach for the best complexity requires designing the strongly monotone solver with the gradient mapping guarantee (see Algorithm 3 and Corollary 2.1). After this, we will invoke this result on a perturbed problem where the initial strong monotonicity level will depend on the desired accuracy, see (2.2), case 2.

Strongly convex subsolver – Algorithm 2.

The first layer was described in the previous section where we solve a sequence of strongly monotone subproblems. To solve these problems, we use a restarting-based second layer (Algorithm 2) similar to AZ (18). This method restarts Algorithm 1 with two different step size and inner iteration limit pairs.

Main workhorse: Anchored stochastic extragradient – Algorithm 1.

Anchoring is mainly used to handle the BG variance assumption (Assumption 2). Indeed, if the variance is bounded, then B=0B=0 and the algorithm reduces to regular stochastic extragradient method. However, the anchoring allows us to handle nonzero BB, to cover problems without bounded variance.

We now continue with the summary of two main results that will be developed in the sequel.

2.1 Complexity for Strongly Monotone Problems

We now state the main complexity results for solving strongly monotone problems, which correspond to strongly convex-strongly concave instances of (1.1). We state this result under bounded variance, since we don’t prove it under Blum-Gladyshev variance due to space constraints. The following result is proven in Section 4.1. A similar result under BG variance assumption can be proven by using the tools in Section 5. We omit this extension for brevity.

Corollary 2.1.

For problem (MI), let Assumption 1 hold and suppose that Assumption 2 holds with B=0B=0. Additionally assume that FF is μF\mu_{F}-strongly monotone. Let S=⌊log2⁡(LF/μF)⌋≥1S=\lfloor\log_{2}(L_{F}/\mu_{F})\rfloor\geq 1, T≥48​S​LF/μFT\geq 48SL_{F}/\mu_{F} and η=13​LF\eta=\frac{1}{3L_{F}}. Then, we have that

𝔼​‖𝒢η,H​(𝐳S)‖≤ε,\mathbb{E}\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H}(\mathbf{z}_{S})\|\leq\varepsilon, (2.4)

where the number of stochastic first-order oracles TT is upper bounded by

O⁡(LFμF​log⁡(LFμF)​log⁡(μF​D⋆ε+e)+G2​log3⁡(LF/μF)ε2).O\left(\frac{L_{F}}{\mu_{F}}\log\left(\frac{L_{F}}{\mu_{F}}\right)\log\left(\frac{\mu_{F}D_{\star}}{\varepsilon}+e\right)+\frac{G^{2}\log^{3}(L_{F}/\mu_{F})}{\varepsilon^{2}}\right).

where OO only suppresses the absolute constants.

Even for unconstrained problems, our result extends (CL, 24, Theorem 4.1) since our algorithmic parameters do not depend on ‖𝐳0−𝐱⋆‖\|\mathbf{z}_{0}-\mathbf{x}^{\star}\| or a global variance upper bound σ2\sigma^{2}, which were required for running the algorithm in (CL, 24, Theorem 4.1). The parameters in our algorithm only depend on the oracle budget TT, LFL_{F} and μF\mu_{F}.

2.2 Complexity for Monotone Problems

By using the result for the strongly monotone case with a perturbed version of the monotone problem, we can obtain the claimed complexity guarantee for solving the original monotone problem. For this we need to connect the solutions in terms of the gradient mapping norm and use the previous result. In particular, we will solve

find ​𝐳0⋆​ such that ​0∈Hμ​(𝐳0⋆):=F⁡(𝐳0⋆)+∂r⁡(𝐳0⋆)+μ⁡(𝐳0⋆−𝐳̊),\text{find~}\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{0}\text{~such that~}0\in H^{\mu}(\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{0}):=F(\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{0})+\partial r(\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{0})+\mu(\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{0}-\mathring{\mathbf{z}}), (2.5)

where μ=O~​(1T)\mu=\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}\right). Since μ\mu is small depending on the oracle budget TT, the perturbed problem is sufficiently close to the original problem to yield the claimed complexity result on the gradient mapping. The proof of the following result is the focus of Section 5.

Corollary 2.2.

For problem (MI), let Assumptions 1 and 2 hold. We apply Algorithm 3 to solve (2.1) with μ=32​L^FT​log23/2⁡(T48)\mu=\frac{32\widehat{L}_{F}}{\sqrt{T}}\log_{2}^{3/2}\left(\frac{\sqrt{T}}{48}\right), T≥14175T\geq 14175, η=13​L^F\eta=\frac{1}{3\widehat{L}_{F}}. Then, we have that

𝔼​‖𝒢η,H​(𝐳S)‖=O⁡(L^F​D⋆​(ln⁡T)3/2T+(ln⁡T)5/2​(B​D⋆+G)T).\mathbb{E}\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H}(\mathbf{z}_{S})\|=O\left(\frac{\widehat{L}_{F}D_{\star}(\ln\sqrt{T})^{3/2}}{\sqrt{T}}+\frac{(\ln\sqrt{T})^{5/2}(BD_{\star}+G)}{\sqrt{T}}\right). (2.6)

Consequently, to obtain

𝔼​‖𝒢η,H​(𝐳S)‖≤ε,\mathbb{E}\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H}(\mathbf{z}_{S})\|\leq\varepsilon, (2.7)

the number of required stochastic first-order oracles TT is upper bounded by

O⁡(1+(LF2+B2)​D⋆2+G2ε2​ln5⁡(D⋆​(LF+B)+Gε+1)),O\left(1+\frac{(L_{F}^{2}+B^{2})D_{\star}^{2}+G^{2}}{\varepsilon^{2}}\ln^{5}\left(\frac{D_{\star}(L_{F}+B)+G}{\varepsilon}+1\right)\right),

where we only suppress the absolute constants.

A similar discussion as the previous subsection apply here to compare our result with the corresponding result of CL (24). In particular, we not only improve over this result to handle constrained or regularized problems, but also require a weaker variance assumption, and use algorithmic parameters only depending on LF,T,BL_{F},T,B. An additional point of discussion is the parameter μ\mu, which is independent of ‖𝐳̊−𝐱⋆‖2\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{x}^{\star}\|^{2}, whereas this quantity was used to set μ\mu in the work of CL (24). To transfer our guarantees to a guarantee on the stronger tangent residual (see its definition, e.g., in COZ (22)), one can apply a postprocessing step similar to (CAD, 24, Appendix C.3).

3 Analysis for Subsolvers

3.1 Layer 1: Anchored Stochastic Extragradient

We now analyze Alg. 1 which is the main workhorse of the construction. It is an extragradient-based method for solving a strongly monotone inclusion problem. The addition on top of the standard extragradient is the Halpern-type anchoring step Hal (67).

Even though we are not aware of this algorithm being proposed or analyzed before; in spirit, it can be considered as a stochastic version of regular anchored extragradient (see YR (21) and (KG, 22, Algorithm 3)) or a single-sample version of LK (21), or non-variance reduced version of (AMW, 25, Section 4.3). Our choice for building on extragradient is purely for presentation purposes, as similar bounds can be proven for anchored versions of other algorithms.

All these works above focused on the non-strongly monotone case. However, our subproblems are strongly monotone, so we analyze for this case. We will call this method and its complexity result for a series of subproblems, so we introduce the problem:

find ​𝐱A⋆​ such that ​0∈(A+∂r)​(𝐱A⋆),\displaystyle\text{find~}\mathbf{x}^{\star}_{A}\text{~such that~}0\in(A+\partial r)(\mathbf{x}^{\star}_{A}), (3.1)

when AA is strongly monotone. At each step ss of Algorithm 3, we will change AA depending on Fs−1F^{s-1}, see (2.3).

For convenience, let us introduce the assumptions to be used in this and next subsection.

Assumption 3.

For problem (3.1), let AA be monotone, LAL_{A}-Lipschitz and μA\mu_{A}-strongly monotone. Assume that rr is proper, convex, closed. There exists 𝐱A⋆\mathbf{x}^{\star}_{A} such that 0∈(A+∂r)​(𝐱A⋆)0\in(A+\partial r)(\mathbf{x}^{\star}_{A}).

We have access to an unbiased estimator of AA such that 𝔼⁡[Aξ​(𝐱)]=A⁡(𝐱)\mathbb{E}[A_{\xi}(\mathbf{x})]=A(\mathbf{x}) and

𝔼​‖Aξ​(𝐱)−A⁡(𝐱)‖2≤BA2​‖𝐱−𝐳̊‖2+GA2,\mathbb{E}\|A_{\xi}(\mathbf{x})-A(\mathbf{x})\|^{2}\leq B_{A}^{2}\|\mathbf{x}-\mathring{\mathbf{z}}\|^{2}+G_{A}^{2},

where 𝐳̊\mathring{\mathbf{z}} is a globally fixed iterate.

To see the connection between the parameters BA,GAB_{A},G_{A} of the variance assumption in this section and the variance assumption made for the global problem (Assumption 2), see Fact 6.5.

The following lemma, when β=0\beta=0 is completely classical, see JNT (11) for an early reference. We provide a generalization here with the anchoring step. We build on NO (24); AMW (25) who analyzed similar algorithms in different contexts, without strong monotonicity. The main idea is to use the anchoring with weight β\beta to absorb the contribution coming from the iterate-dependent BAB_{A} term in the BG assumption (Assumption 3), which allows relaxing the bounded variance assumption.

Lemma 3.1.

For problem (3.1), let Assumption 3 hold. When we run Algorithm 1 for KK iterations, with parameters α≤12​(LA+BA)\alpha\leq\frac{1}{2(L_{A}+B_{A})}, β=3​α2​BA2\beta=3\alpha^{2}B_{A}^{2}, we obtain

𝔼​‖𝐱^Ks,n−𝐱A⋆‖2≤12​α​μA​K​‖𝐱0s,n−𝐱A⋆‖2+3​αμA​(BA2​‖𝐳̊−𝐱A⋆‖2+7​GA218).\mathbb{E}\|\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{K}^{s,n}-\mathbf{x}^{\star}_{A}\|^{2}\leq\frac{1}{2\alpha\mu_{A}K}\|\mathbf{x}_{0}^{s,n}-\mathbf{x}^{\star}_{A}\|^{2}+\frac{3\alpha}{\mu_{A}}\left(B_{A}^{2}\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{x}^{\star}_{A}\|^{2}+\frac{7G_{A}^{2}}{18}\right).
Remark 3.2.

In this bound, the additional term BA2​‖𝐳̊−𝐱A⋆‖2B^{2}_{A}\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{x}^{\star}_{A}\|^{2} coming from the relaxed variance requirement seems not problematic since 𝐱A⋆\mathbf{x}^{\star}_{A} is fixed. However, we will later invoke this result with a dynamic set of problems where the solution 𝐱A⋆\mathbf{x}^{\star}_{A} will be changing at each step. As a result, we cannot treat this term as a constant. We will have to craft a specialized analysis to handle this additional term since we do not have a global upper bound for the solutions of inner problems. This will be handled in Section 5.

For a lighter notation, we suppress the superscript s,ns,n from the iterates, as in the algorithm.

By the update rules of the iterates 𝐱k+1/2,𝐱k+1\mathbf{x}_{k+1/2},\mathbf{x}_{k+1} in Algorithm 1, and (1.7), we have

≥𝔼⁡[r⁡(𝐱A⋆)−r⁡(𝐱k+1/2)+μA​‖𝐱A⋆−𝐱k+1/2‖2],\displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}[r(\mathbf{x}^{\star}_{A})-r(\mathbf{x}_{k+1/2})+\mu_{A}\|\mathbf{x}^{\star}_{A}-\mathbf{x}_{k+1/2}\|^{2}], (3.5)

The following result analyzes the restart-based instantiations of the inner solver and the argument is the same as AZ (18) (see also HK (14)), invoked with slightly different parameters and constants.

4 Complexity Analysis with Bounded Variance

We now analyze Algorithm 3. This method calls Algorithm 2 repeatedly for SS times where each step approximates the problem in (2.3).

For analyzing this scheme, we will invoke Lemma 3.3, with 𝐱A⋆←𝐳s−1⋆\mathbf{x}_{A}^{\star}\leftarrow\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{s-1} and 𝐲0←𝐳s−1\mathbf{y}_{0}\leftarrow\mathbf{z}_{s-1}. Since the last term on the right-hand side of the result of Lemma 3.3 has a term depending on B2​‖𝐳̊−𝐳s−1⋆‖2B^{2}\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}\|^{2}, we need a dedicated analysis to control this term since such a term did not exist in prior analyses that required a uniformly bounded variance (CL, 24; AZ, 18). For simplicity, we will first analyze the case B=0B=0 which corresponds to bounded variance and then we will show how to handle the B≠0B\neq 0 case in the next section.

The two results below will be used for both monotone and strongly monotone cases. As a result, they only use that FμF^{\mu} is μ\mu-strongly monotone which is true in both cases, due to the definition (2.2).

For problem (MI), let Assumption 1 hold and suppose that Assumption 2 holds with B=0B=0. We apply Algorithm 3 to solve (2.1) with budget T≥48​κ​ST\geq 48\kappa S for number of oracles where κ=LFμ\kappa=\frac{L_{F}}{\mu}, S=⌊log2⁡κ⌋≥1S=\left\lfloor\log_{2}\kappa\right\rfloor\geq 1 and initial point 𝐳̊\mathring{\mathbf{z}}. We have for all s=1,…,Ss=1,\dots,S that

μs2​𝔼​‖𝐳s−𝐳s−1⋆‖2≤(12)T​s24​κ​S​μ2​‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖2+400​S​G2T,\displaystyle\mu_{s}^{2}\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{z}_{s}-\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}\|^{2}\leq\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{Ts}{24\kappa S}}\mu^{2}\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{0}\|^{2}+\frac{400SG^{2}}{T},

and the points 𝐳s⋆\mathbf{z}_{s}^{\star} are as defined in (2.3).

μA←(2s−1)​μ,L^A≡LA←LF+(2s−1)​μ,L^AμA=LF+(2s−1)​μ(2s−1)​μ≤3​κ2,BA←0,GA←G,\mu_{A}\leftarrow(2^{s}-1)\mu,~~~\widehat{L}_{A}\equiv L_{A}\leftarrow L_{F}+(2^{s}-1)\mu,~~~\frac{\widehat{L}_{A}}{\mu_{A}}=\frac{L_{F}+(2^{s}-1)\mu}{(2^{s}-1)\mu}\leq\frac{3\kappa}{2},~~~B_{A}\leftarrow 0,~~~G_{A}\leftarrow G, (4.2)

where we used 4​(12)T12​κ​S≤(12)T24​κ​S4\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{T}{12\kappa S}}\leq\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{T}{24\kappa S}} due to T≥48​κ​ST\geq 48\kappa S.

Using Lemma 6.1 and μs2=4​μs−12\mu_{s}^{2}=4\mu_{s-1}^{2}, this implies that for s≥2s\geq 2:

≤(12)s​T24​S​κ​μ2​‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖2+300​S​G2T​∑i=0s−1(12)i​T24​κ​S,\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{sT}{24S\kappa}}\mu^{2}\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}\|^{2}+\frac{300SG^{2}}{T}\sum_{i=0}^{s-1}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{iT}{24\kappa S}},

By using Lemma 6.4, we can now convert this result to a guarantee on the gradient mapping norm for the operator HμH^{\mu} given in (2.1). In view of its definition, this will directly give us the required guarantee for the strongly monotone setting. In the monotone setting, we will select μ\mu accordingly to get a guarantee for the original problem in (MI).

Lemma 4.2.

For problem (MI), let Assumption 1 hold and suppose that Assumption 2 holds with B=0B=0. 4.1 Strongly Monotone Case

In the strongly monotone case, we will use the first case in the definition of FμF^{\mu} in (2.2). This reduces HμH^{\mu} to the original problem and we have the following theorem as the direct corollary of Lemma 4.2.

Theorem 4.3.

For problem (MI), let Assumption 1 hold and suppose that Assumption 2 holds with B=0B=0. Additionally assume that FF is μF\mu_{F} strongly monotone for μF>0\mu_{F}>0. We apply Algorithm 3 to solve (2.1) with η=13​LF\eta=\frac{1}{3L_{F}}, S=⌊log2⁡(LF/μF)⌋≥1S=\lfloor\log_{2}(L_{F}/\mu_{F})\rfloor\geq 1 and T≥48​S​LF/μFT\geq 48SL_{F}/\mu_{F}, and initial point 𝐳̊\mathring{\mathbf{z}}. Then, we have that

𝔼​‖𝒢η,H​(𝐳S)‖=O⁡((12)T48​S​LF/μF​μF​D⋆+S3/2​GT),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H}(\mathbf{z}_{S})\|=O\left(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{T}{48SL_{F}/\mu_{F}}}\mu_{F}D_{\star}+\frac{S^{3/2}G}{\sqrt{T}}\right),

where OO only suppresses the absolute constants.

Since FF is strongly monotone, in view of (2.2), we have Fμ=FF^{\mu}=F, μ=μF\mu=\mu_{F}, and 𝐳0⋆=𝐱⋆\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}=\mathbf{x}^{\star}. Then, we invoke Lemma 4.2 with these settings and use the definition of D⋆D_{\star} from (1.8) to derive the bound. ∎

The next corollary then immediately follows by finding the value of TT to make the right-hand side of Theorem 4.3 less than ε\varepsilon.

Corollary 4.4.

Under the same setup as Theorem 4.3, we have

𝔼​‖𝒢η,H​(𝐳S)‖≤ε,\mathbb{E}\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H}(\mathbf{z}_{S})\|\leq\varepsilon, (4.5)

where the number of stochastic first-order oracles TT is upper bounded by

O⁡(LFμF​log⁡(LFμF)​log⁡(μF​D⋆ε+e)+G2​log3⁡(LF/μF)ε2).O\left(\frac{L_{F}}{\mu_{F}}\log\left(\frac{L_{F}}{\mu_{F}}\right)\log\left(\frac{\mu_{F}D_{\star}}{\varepsilon}+e\right)+\frac{G^{2}\log^{3}(L_{F}/\mu_{F})}{\varepsilon^{2}}\right).

Our algorithmic parameters do not depend on ‖𝐳0−𝐱⋆‖\|\mathbf{z}_{0}-\mathbf{x}^{\star}\| or a global variance upper bound σ2\sigma^{2}, which were required for running the algorithm in (CL, 24, Theorem 4.1). The parameters in our algorithm only depend on the oracle budget TT, LFL_{F} and μF\mu_{F}, similar to the case of AZ (18) in the minimization case and the bound for the gradient mapping in Theorem 4.3 follows. Converting this to a complexity bound gives Corollary 4.4.

4.2 Monotone Case

In view of the definitions in (2.1) and (2.2), we are in the second case of (2.2). Let us recall that Lemma 4.2 gives a bound for solving the perturbed problem, controlled by μ\mu. By controlling μ\mu and the distance between gradient mapping at perturbed problem and the original problem, we will derive a guarantee for the gradient mapping for solving the original problem in (MI).

Theorem 4.5 (Monotone FF).

For problem (MI), let Assumption 1 hold and suppose that Assumption 2 holds with B=0B=0. We apply Algorithm 3 to solve (2.1) with any LF/2≥μ>0L_{F}/2\geq\mu>0, η=13​LF\eta=\frac{1}{3L_{F}}, S=⌊log2⁡(LF/μ)⌋≥1S=\lfloor\log_{2}(L_{F}/\mu)\rfloor\geq 1 and T≥48​S​LF/μT\geq 48SL_{F}/\mu, and initial point 𝐳̊\mathring{\mathbf{z}}. Then, we have that

𝔼​‖𝒢η,H​(𝐳S)‖=O⁡(μ​‖𝐱⋆−𝐳̊‖+(12)T48​S​LF/μ​μ​‖𝐳̊−𝐱⋆‖+S3/2​GT).\mathbb{E}\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H}(\mathbf{z}_{S})\|=O\left(\mu\|\mathbf{x}^{\star}-\mathring{\mathbf{z}}\|+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{T}{48SL_{F}/\mu}}\mu\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{x}^{\star}\|+\frac{S^{3/2}G}{\sqrt{T}}\right).
Proof.

Applying Lemma 6.3 yields the inequality

‖𝒢η,H​(𝐳S)‖≤2.5​∑j=1Sμj​‖𝐳j−𝐳j−1⋆‖+9​LF​‖𝐳S−𝐳S−1⋆‖+μ​‖𝐳̊−𝐱⋆‖.\displaystyle\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H}(\mathbf{z}_{S})\|\leq 2.5\sum_{j=1}^{S}\mu_{j}\|\mathbf{z}_{j}-\mathbf{z}_{j-1}^{\star}\|+9L_{F}\|\mathbf{z}_{S}-\mathbf{z}_{S-1}^{\star}\|+\mu\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{x}^{\star}\|. (4.6)

Since Lemma 4.1 holds in this case, on (4.6), we use (6.11) to bound the first term and (6.12) the second term on the right-hand side and use (6.8) to obtain the claimed bound. ∎

Corollary 4.6.

Under the same setup of Theorem 4.5, let T≥2200T\geq 2200 and μ=96​LF​log2​TT\mu=\frac{96L_{F}\log_{2}T}{T}. We apply Algorithm 3 to solve (2.1) with η=13​LF\eta=\frac{1}{3L_{F}}, S=⌊log2⁡(LF/μ)⌋S=\lfloor\log_{2}(L_{F}/\mu)\rfloor, and initial point 𝐳̊\mathring{\mathbf{z}}. Then, we have that

𝔼​‖𝒢η,H​(𝐳S)‖=O⁡(LF​D⋆​log2​TT+G​(log2⁡T)3/2T).\mathbb{E}\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H}(\mathbf{z}_{S})\|=O\left(\frac{L_{F}D_{\star}\log_{2}T}{T}+\frac{G(\log_{2}T)^{3/2}}{\sqrt{T}}\right). (4.7)

Consequently, to obtain

𝔼​‖𝒢η,H​(𝐳S)‖≤ε,\mathbb{E}\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H}(\mathbf{z}_{S})\|\leq\varepsilon, (4.8)

the required number of stochastic first-order oracles TT is upper bounded by

O⁡(1+LF​D⋆ε​ln⁡(LF​D⋆ε+1)+G2ε2​ln3⁡(Gε+1)),O\left(1+\frac{L_{F}D_{\star}}{\varepsilon}\ln\left(\frac{L_{F}D_{\star}}{\varepsilon}+1\right)+\frac{G^{2}}{\varepsilon^{2}}\ln^{3}\left(\frac{G}{\varepsilon}+1\right)\right),

where we only suppress the absolute constants.

Proof.

In this case, we start from the result of Lemma 6.3, after plugging in from (6.11) and (6.12) to derive

𝔼​‖𝒢η,H​(𝐳S)‖≤μ​D⋆+5​(12)T48​κ​S​μ​D⋆+50​S3/2​GT+18​((12)T48​κ​μ​D⋆+20​S​GT),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H}(\mathbf{z}_{S})\|\leq\mu D_{\star}+5\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{T}{48\kappa S}}\mu D_{\star}+\frac{50S^{3/2}G}{\sqrt{T}}+18\bigg(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{T}{48\kappa}}\mu D_{\star}+\frac{20\sqrt{S}G}{\sqrt{T}}\bigg), (4.9)

where we also used Lemma 6.1 which gives ‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖≤‖𝐳̊−𝐱⋆‖=D⋆\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{0}\|\leq\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{x}^{\star}\|=D_{\star}. Plugging in the definition of μ\mu gives (4.7). From this bound, it should be clear that this choice of μ\mu will give a complexity result scaling as ε−2\varepsilon^{-2} up to logarithmic terms. First, we verify that the requirement on TT in Theorem 4.5 is satisfied. That is, we show that T≥48​κ​ST\geq 48\kappa S. 48​κ​S=T2​log2​T​S≤T.\displaystyle 48\kappa S=\frac{T}{2\log_{2}T}S\leq T.

Moreover, by the definition of κ\kappa, we also have that κ≥2\kappa\geq 2 since T≥2200T\geq 2200.

Because of this requirement, for making the first, second and fourth terms in (4.9) less than ε\varepsilon, we need μ​D⋆≤ε/9\mu D_{\star}\leq\varepsilon/9. This is true when

96​LF​D⋆​log2​TT≤ε9,\displaystyle\frac{96L_{F}D_{\star}\log_{2}T}{T}\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{9},

which is true for T=Θ⁡(LF​D⋆ε​ln⁡(LF​D⋆ε+1))T=\Theta\left(\frac{L_{F}D_{\star}}{\varepsilon}\ln\left(\frac{L_{F}D_{\star}}{\varepsilon}+1\right)\right) because of Lemma 6.7(ii) with a=96​LF​D⋆a=96L_{F}D_{\star}, b=1b=1, c=1c=1. ε′=ε/9\varepsilon^{\prime}=\varepsilon/9.

We finally calculate the order of TT to make the third and fifth terms on the right-hand side of (4.9) less than ε\varepsilon. Since the third term dominates the fifth up to absolute constants, we calculate TT to make

50​S3/2​GT≤ε,\displaystyle\frac{50S^{3/2}G}{\sqrt{T}}\leq\varepsilon,

where S=⌊log2⁡LFμ⌋≤log2⁡LFμ≤log2⁡TS=\left\lfloor\log_{2}\frac{L_{F}}{\mu}\right\rfloor\leq\log_{2}\frac{L_{F}}{\mu}\leq\log_{2}T. As a result, a sufficient condition is

2500​G2​(log2⁡T)3T≤ε2,\displaystyle\frac{2500G^{2}(\log_{2}T)^{3}}{T}\leq\varepsilon^{2},

which is true for T=Θ⁡(G2ε2​ln3⁡(Gε+1))T=\Theta\left(\frac{G^{2}}{\varepsilon^{2}}\ln^{3}\left(\frac{G}{\varepsilon}+1\right)\right) because of Lemma 6.7(ii) with a=2500​G2a=2500G^{2}, b=1b=1, c=3c=3. ε′=ε2\varepsilon^{\prime}=\varepsilon^{2}.

Combining the two bounds for TT gives the assertion. ∎

5 Complexity Analysis without Bounded Variance

For brevity, we will only analyze the monotone case, the strongly monotone case can be analyzed similarly by replacing the μ\mu value by the strong monotonicity of the operator.

We now derive the result corresponding to Lemma 4.1 when the bounded variance assumption is lifted. Even for unconstrained problems, our result extends (CL, 24, Theorem 4.1) in that we do not require a globally upper bounded variance, but only Assumption 2.

Lemma 5.1.

For problem (MI), let Assumption 1 and Assumption 2 hold. We apply Algorithm 3 to solve (2.1) with budget T≥14175T\geq 14175 for number of oracles, μ=32​L^FT​log23/2​T48\mu=\frac{32\widehat{L}_{F}}{\sqrt{T}}\log_{2}^{3/2}\frac{\sqrt{T}}{48} and initial point 𝐳̊\mathring{\mathbf{z}}. We have for all s=1,…,Ss=1,\dots,S that

μs2​𝔼​‖𝐳s−𝐳s−1⋆‖2≤(12)T​s24​κ​S​μ2​‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖2+2048​S3​G^2T,\displaystyle\mu_{s}^{2}\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{z}_{s}-\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}\|^{2}\leq\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{Ts}{24\kappa S}}\mu^{2}\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{0}\|^{2}+\frac{2048S^{3}\widehat{G}^{2}}{T},

With these settings, we can verify that the requirements of Assumption 3 hold. Then, we will get the structural constants in the setting of Lemma 3.3 becoming

μA←(2s−1)μ,LA←Ls−1=LF+(2s−1)μ,BA←B,GA←G,\mu_{A}\leftarrow(2^{s}-1)\mu_{,}~~~L_{A}\leftarrow L_{s-1}=L_{F}+(2^{s}-1)\mu,~~~B_{A}\leftarrow B,~~~G_{A}\leftarrow G, (5.2)

where we use Fact 6.5. As a result, from Lemma 3.3, we have for s≥1s\geq 1:

𝔼​‖𝐳s−𝐳s−1⋆‖2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{z}_{s}-\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}\|^{2} ≤(12)T12​S​κ​𝔼​‖𝐳s−1−𝐳s−1⋆‖2+192​S​𝔼​(B2​‖𝐳̊−𝐳s−1⋆‖2+G2)T​μs−12,\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{T}{12S\kappa}}\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{z}_{s-1}-\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}\|^{2}+\frac{192S\mathbb{E}(B^{2}\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{s-1}\|^{2}+G^{2})}{T\mu_{s-1}^{2}}, (5.3)

since μs−1≤μA\mu_{s-1}\leq\mu_{A}. Here, we also majorized the constant in the last term for simplicity.

‖𝐳̊−𝐳s−1⋆‖\displaystyle\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}\| ≤‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖+∑j=1s−1‖𝐳j⋆−𝐳j−1⋆‖≤‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖+∑j=1s−1‖𝐳j−𝐳j−1⋆‖.\displaystyle\leq\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}\|+\sum_{j=1}^{s-1}\|\mathbf{z}_{j}^{\star}-\mathbf{z}_{j-1}^{\star}\|\leq\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}\|+\sum_{j=1}^{s-1}\|\mathbf{z}_{j}-\mathbf{z}_{j-1}^{\star}\|.

‖𝐳̊−𝐳s−1⋆‖2≤S​‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖2+S​∑j=1s−1‖𝐳j−𝐳j−1⋆‖2,\displaystyle\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}\|^{2}\leq S\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}\|^{2}+S\sum_{j=1}^{s-1}\|\mathbf{z}_{j}-\mathbf{z}_{j-1}^{\star}\|^{2}, (5.4)

since s≤Ss\leq S.

Using this bound and Lemma 6.1 on (5.3) yields for s≥2s\geq 2,

𝔼​‖𝐳s−𝐳s−1⋆‖2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{z}_{s}-\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}\|^{2} ≤(12)T12​S​κ​𝔼​‖𝐳s−1−𝐳s−2⋆‖2+192​S2​B2​(‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖2+∑j=1s−1𝔼​‖𝐳j−𝐳j−1⋆‖2)T​μs−12+192​S​G2T​μs−12.\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{T}{12S\kappa}}\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{z}_{s-1}-\mathbf{z}_{s-2}^{\star}\|^{2}+\frac{192S^{2}B^{2}(\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}\|^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{s-1}\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{z}_{j}-\mathbf{z}_{j-1}^{\star}\|^{2})}{T\mu_{s-1}^{2}}+\frac{192SG^{2}}{T\mu_{s-1}^{2}}. (5.5)

Due to Lemma 6.7(iii), the choice of TT and μ\mu implies that

T≥48​κ​S,μ2≥1024​S3​L^F2T.T\geq 48\kappa S,\qquad\mu^{2}\geq\frac{1024S^{3}\widehat{L}_{F}^{2}}{T}.

As a result, we notice for the coefficients in (5.5) that

(12)T12​S​κ≤14​, ​192​S2​B2T​μs−12≤256​S2​B2T​μ2≤14​S, ​192​S​G2T​μs−12≤G24​(LF+B)2​S2≤G24​(LF+B)2,\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{T}{12S\kappa}}\leq\frac{1}{4}\text{,~~~}\frac{192S^{2}B^{2}}{T\mu_{s-1}^{2}}\leq\frac{256S^{2}B^{2}}{T\mu^{2}}\leq\frac{1}{4S},\text{~~~}\frac{192SG^{2}}{T\mu_{s-1}^{2}}\leq\frac{G^{2}}{4(L_{F}+B)^{2}S^{2}}\leq\frac{G^{2}}{4(L_{F}+B)^{2}}, (5.6)

where we also used μs−1≥μ\mu_{s-1}\geq\mu and S≥1S\geq 1.

We will next use induction. With these estimates, the inequality (5.5) becomes for s≥2s\geq 2

𝔼​‖𝐳s−𝐳s−1⋆‖2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{z}_{s}-\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}\|^{2} ≤14​𝔼​‖𝐳s−1−𝐳s−2⋆‖2+‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖2+∑j=1s−1𝔼​‖𝐳j−𝐳j−1⋆‖24​S+G24​(LF+B)2.\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{4}\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{z}_{s-1}-\mathbf{z}_{s-2}^{\star}\|^{2}+\frac{\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}\|^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{s-1}\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{z}_{j}-\mathbf{z}_{j-1}^{\star}\|^{2}}{4S}+\frac{G^{2}}{4(L_{F}+B)^{2}}. (5.7)

For s=1s=1, from (5.3), with 𝐳0=𝐳̊\mathbf{z}_{0}=\mathring{\mathbf{z}} and 𝐳s−1⋆=𝐳0⋆\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}=\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}, we have

𝔼​‖𝐳1−𝐳0⋆‖2≤(12)T12​S​κ​‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖2+192​S​(B2​‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖2+G2)T​μ02.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{z}_{1}-\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}\|^{2}\leq\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{T}{12S\kappa}}\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}\|^{2}+\frac{192S(B^{2}\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}\|^{2}+G^{2})}{T\mu_{0}^{2}}.

Applying (5.4) and (5.6) gives

𝔼​‖𝐳1−𝐳0⋆‖2≤14​‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖2+‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖24​S+G24​(LF+B)2.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{z}_{1}-\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}\|^{2}\leq\frac{1}{4}\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}\|^{2}+\frac{\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}\|^{2}}{4S}+\frac{G^{2}}{4(L_{F}+B)^{2}}.

We will prove 𝔼​‖𝐳j−𝐳j−1⋆‖2≤‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖2+G2(LF+B)2\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{z}_{j}-\mathbf{z}_{j-1}^{\star}\|^{2}\leq\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}\|^{2}+\frac{G^{2}}{(L_{F}+B)^{2}} for j≥1j\geq 1. By the last display equation, the claim holds at j=1j=1. Assume that it holds for j≤s−1j\leq s-1 with s≥2s\geq 2. Then, (5.7) gives

𝔼​‖𝐳s−𝐳s−1⋆‖2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{z}_{s}-\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}\|^{2} ≤12​(‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖2+G2(LF+B)2)+G24​(LF+B)2\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\left(\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}\|^{2}+\frac{G^{2}}{(L_{F}+B)^{2}}\right)+\frac{G^{2}}{4(L_{F}+B)^{2}}
≤‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖2+G2(LF+B)2.\displaystyle\leq\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}\|^{2}+\frac{G^{2}}{(L_{F}+B)^{2}}. (5.8)

Then, using (5.4) and taking expectation, we have

𝔼​‖𝐳̊−𝐳s−1⋆‖2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}\|^{2} ≤S​‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖2+S​∑j=1s−1(‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖2+G2(LF+B)2)\displaystyle\leq S\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}\|^{2}+S\sum_{j=1}^{s-1}\left(\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}\|^{2}+\frac{G^{2}}{(L_{F}+B)^{2}}\right)
≤2​S2​‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖2+S2​G2(LF+B)2.\displaystyle\leq 2S^{2}\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}\|^{2}+\frac{S^{2}G^{2}}{(L_{F}+B)^{2}}.

We now plug this bound to (5.3) which gives us the bound

≤(12)T12​S​κ​𝔼​‖𝐳s−1−𝐳s−1⋆‖2+384​S3​(B2​‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖2+G2)T​μs−12\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{T}{12S\kappa}}\mathbb{E}\|\mathbf{z}_{s-1}-\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}\|^{2}+\frac{384S^{3}(B^{2}\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}\|^{2}+G^{2})}{T\mu_{s-1}^{2}} (5.10)

We follow the exact same steps that followed (4.3) (where the difference is having 384​S3384S^{3} instead of 75​S75S and B2​‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖2+G2B^{2}\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}\|^{2}+G^{2} instead of G2G^{2} on the last term) to get the assertion. ∎

Let us remark that the induction argument in this proof to bound 𝔼​‖𝐳̊−𝐳s−1⋆‖2\mathbb{E}\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}\|^{2} can be strengthened with a more involved analysis to improve the order of the SS term in the final bound. However we chose the current argument for simplicity, since this order only affects the order of the logarithmic terms in the final bound in the sequel.

The next result corresponds to Lemma 4.2 and Theorem 4.5 without the bounded variance assumption.

Theorem 5.2.

For problem (MI), let Assumptions 1 and 2 hold. We apply Algorithm 3 to solve (2.1) with

μ=32​L^FT​log23/2⁡(T48),η=13​L^F,S=⌊log2⁡(L^F/μ)⌋,T≥14175,\mu=\frac{32\widehat{L}_{F}}{\sqrt{T}}\log_{2}^{3/2}\left(\frac{\sqrt{T}}{48}\right),~~~\eta=\frac{1}{3\widehat{L}_{F}},~~~S=\lfloor\log_{2}(\widehat{L}_{F}/\mu)\rfloor,~~~T\geq 14175,

and initial point 𝐳̊\mathring{\mathbf{z}}. Then, we have that

𝔼​‖𝒢η,H​(𝐳S)‖=O⁡(μ​D⋆+(12)T48​S​L^F/μ​μ​D⋆+S5/2​(B​D⋆+G)T).\mathbb{E}\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H}(\mathbf{z}_{S})\|=O\left(\mu D_{\star}+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{T}{48S\widehat{L}_{F}/\mu}}\mu D_{\star}+\frac{S^{5/2}\left(BD_{\star}+G\right)}{\sqrt{T}}\right).
Remark 5.3.

By the value of μ=O~​(1T)\mu=\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}\right) and T≥48​S​L^F/μT\geq 48S\widehat{L}_{F}/\mu as shown in Lemma 6.7, one can estimate that the complexity will be of the order ε−2\varepsilon^{-2} up to logarithmic terms. We follow by a corollary for the order of the terms and then we give the precise constants.

Proof.

The result of Lemma 5.1 shows that the hypothesis of Lemma 6.4 is satisfied with

C=2048​S2​ and ​G^2=B2​‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖2+G2.C=2048S^{2}\text{~~~and~~~}\widehat{G}^{2}=B^{2}\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}\|^{2}+G^{2}. (5.11)

We also know that applying Lemma 6.3 yields the inequality

6 Auxiliary Lemmas

In this section, we will prove auxiliary results that were used in the main proofs. The first result connects the solutions of subproblems for different regularization levels.

Given F0=FμF^{0}=F^{\mu}, let us recall that at iteration s≥1s\geq 1, we estimate 𝐳s−1⋆\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{s-1} such that 0∈(Fs−1+∂r)​(𝐳s−1⋆)0\in(F^{s-1}+\partial r)(\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{s-1}) where

Fs−1(𝐳)=Fμ(𝐳)+∑i=1s−1μi(𝐳−𝐳i), for s=1,2,…,S\displaystyle F^{s-1}(\mathbf{z})=F^{\mu}(\mathbf{z})+\sum_{i=1}^{s-1}\mu_{i}(\mathbf{z}-\mathbf{z}_{i}),\text{~for~}s=1,2,\dots,S (6.1)

with 𝐳0⋆\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{0} is as defined in (2.1).

Lemma 6.1.

For s=1,…,Ss=1,\dots,S, if we are given that F0=FμF^{0}=F^{\mu} (see (2.2)), 𝐳s⋆=(Fs+∂r)−1​(0)\mathbf{z}_{s}^{\star}=(F^{s}+\partial r)^{-1}(0) and 𝐳s−1⋆=(Fs−1+∂r)−1​(0)\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}=(F^{s-1}+\partial r)^{-1}(0), where

Fs​(𝐳)=Fs−1​(𝐳)+μs​(𝐳−𝐳s),F^{s}(\mathbf{z})=F^{s-1}(\mathbf{z})+\mu_{s}(\mathbf{z}-\mathbf{z}_{s}), (6.2)

it follows that

‖𝐳s−𝐳s⋆‖≤‖𝐳s−𝐳s−1⋆‖​ and ​‖𝐳s⋆−𝐳s−1⋆‖≤‖𝐳s−𝐳s−1⋆‖.\|\mathbf{z}_{s}-\mathbf{z}_{s}^{\star}\|\leq\|\mathbf{z}_{s}-\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}\|\text{~and~}\|\mathbf{z}_{s}^{\star}-\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}\|\leq\|\mathbf{z}_{s}-\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}\|.

Moreover, we have that ‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖≤‖𝐳̊−𝐱⋆‖\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{0}\|\leq\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{x}^{\star}\|.

Proof.

By definition of the solutions, we have that

0∈(Fs+∂r)​(𝐳s⋆)​ and ​0∈(Fs−1+∂r)​(𝐳s−1⋆)​ where ​Fs​(𝐳s−1⋆)=Fs−1​(𝐳s−1⋆)+μs​(𝐳s−1⋆−𝐳s),0\in(F^{s}+\partial r)(\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{s})\text{~and~}0\in(F^{s-1}+\partial r)(\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star})\text{~where~}F^{s}(\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star})=F^{s-1}(\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star})+\mu_{s}(\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}-\mathbf{z}_{s}),

because of (6.2). Consequently, we have that μs​(𝐳s−1⋆−𝐳s)∈(Fs+∂r)​(𝐳s−1⋆)\mu_{s}(\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}-\mathbf{z}_{s})\in(F^{s}+\partial r)(\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}).

Let us now use that (Fs+∂r)(F^{s}+\partial r) is μs\mu_{s}-strongly monotone to write

μs​⟨𝐳s−𝐳s−1⋆,𝐳s⋆−𝐳s−1⋆⟩≥μs​‖𝐳s⋆−𝐳s−1⋆‖2\displaystyle\mu_{s}\langle\mathbf{z}_{s}-\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star},\mathbf{z}_{s}^{\star}-\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}\rangle\geq\mu_{s}\|\mathbf{z}_{s}^{\star}-\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}\|^{2}
⇔\displaystyle\iff 12​(‖𝐳s−𝐳s−1⋆‖2+‖𝐳s⋆−𝐳s−1⋆‖2−‖𝐳s−𝐳s⋆‖2)≥‖𝐳s⋆−𝐳s−1⋆‖2.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\left(\|\mathbf{z}_{s}-\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}\|^{2}+\|\mathbf{z}_{s}^{\star}-\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}\|^{2}-\|\mathbf{z}_{s}-\mathbf{z}_{s}^{\star}\|^{2}\right)\geq\|\mathbf{z}_{s}^{\star}-\mathbf{z}_{s-1}^{\star}\|^{2}.

Rearranging the final inequality gives both results.

In view of (2.2), if FF is μ\mu-strongly monotone, the last claim holds with equality. Otherwise, we use μ\mu-strong monotonicity of Fμ+∂rF^{\mu}+\partial r as in the first part of the proof, along with

0∈(Fμ+∂r)​(𝐳0⋆),0∈(F+∂r)​(𝐱⋆),Fμ​(𝐱⋆)=F⁡(𝐱⋆)+μ⁡(𝐱⋆−𝐳̊).\displaystyle 0\in(F^{\mu}+\partial r)(\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}),~~~0\in(F+\partial r)(\mathbf{x}^{\star}),~~~F^{\mu}(\mathbf{x}^{\star})=F(\mathbf{x}^{\star})+\mu(\mathbf{x}^{\star}-\mathring{\mathbf{z}}).

This establishes the last inequality in the statement. ∎

This lemma generalizes (CL, 24, Lemma A.1) which was specialized to unconstrained min-max problems. The extension is to handle the multi-valued mapping ∂r\partial r in the definition of subproblems. For this, we keep all the terms on the right-hand side to depend on the quality of approximate subproblem solutions.

Lemma 6.2.

Under Assumptions 1, 2 and the setup of (2.1)–(2.3), set η=13​L^F\eta=\frac{1}{3\widehat{L}_{F}} where L^F=LF+B\widehat{L}_{F}=L_{F}+B. Then, we have

‖𝒢η,Hμ​(𝐳S)‖≤2​∑j=1Sμj​‖𝐳j−𝐳j−1⋆‖+9​L^F​‖𝐳S−𝐳S−1⋆‖,\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H^{\mu}}(\mathbf{z}_{S})\|\leq 2\sum_{j=1}^{S}\mu_{j}\|\mathbf{z}_{j}-\mathbf{z}_{j-1}^{\star}\|+9\widehat{L}_{F}\|\mathbf{z}_{S}-\mathbf{z}_{S-1}^{\star}\|, (6.3)

where μs=2s​μ\mu_{s}=2^{s}\mu and 𝐳s,𝐳s⋆\mathbf{z}_{s},\mathbf{z}_{s}^{\star} are as given in (6.1) (see also (2.3) and (2.1)).

Proof.

We first recall the definition of the residual for operators Hμ=Fμ+∂rH^{\mu}=F^{\mu}+\partial r and Hs=Fs+∂rH^{s}=F^{s}+\partial r, respectively:

𝒢η,Hμ​(𝐳)=η−1​(𝐳−proxη​r⁡(𝐳−η​Fμ​(𝐳)))​ and ​𝒢η,HS−1​(𝐳)=η−1​(𝐳−proxη​r⁡(𝐳−η​FS−1​(𝐳))).\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H^{\mu}}(\mathbf{z})=\eta^{-1}\left(\mathbf{z}-\prox_{\eta r}(\mathbf{z}-\eta F^{\mu}(\mathbf{z}))\right)\text{~~~and~~~}\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H^{S-1}}(\mathbf{z})=\eta^{-1}\left(\mathbf{z}-\prox_{\eta r}(\mathbf{z}-\eta F^{S-1}(\mathbf{z}))\right).

By these definitions, we have

‖𝒢η,Hμ​(𝐳S)−𝒢η,HS−1​(𝐳S)‖\displaystyle\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H^{\mu}}(\mathbf{z}_{S})-\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H^{S-1}}(\mathbf{z}_{S})\| =η−1​‖proxη​r⁡(𝐳S−η​Fμ​(𝐳S))−proxη​r⁡(𝐳S−η​FS−1​(𝐳S))‖\displaystyle=\eta^{-1}\|\prox_{\eta r}(\mathbf{z}_{S}-\eta F^{\mu}(\mathbf{z}_{S}))-\prox_{\eta r}(\mathbf{z}_{S}-\eta F^{S-1}(\mathbf{z}_{S}))\|
≤‖Fμ​(𝐳S)−FS−1​(𝐳S)‖\displaystyle\leq\|F^{\mu}(\mathbf{z}_{S})-F^{S-1}(\mathbf{z}_{S})\|
≤∑i=1S−1μi​‖𝐳S−𝐳i‖,\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{S-1}\mu_{i}\|\mathbf{z}_{S}-\mathbf{z}_{i}\|, (6.4)

where the first inequality used nonexpansiveness of the proximal operator, see for example (Bec, 17, Theorem 6.42). The last inequality is by (6.1) and triangle inequality.

Now we estimate the term on the right-hand side by using triangle inequality and Lemma 6.1

‖𝐳S−𝐳i‖\displaystyle\|\mathbf{z}_{S}-\mathbf{z}_{i}\| ≤‖𝐳S−𝐳S−1⋆‖+∑j=iS−2‖𝐳j+1⋆−𝐳j⋆‖+‖𝐳i⋆−𝐳i‖≤∑j=iS‖𝐳j−𝐳j−1⋆‖.\displaystyle\leq\|\mathbf{z}_{S}-\mathbf{z}_{S-1}^{\star}\|+\sum_{j=i}^{S-2}\|\mathbf{z}_{j+1}^{\star}-\mathbf{z}_{j}^{\star}\|+\|\mathbf{z}_{i}^{\star}-\mathbf{z}_{i}\|\leq\sum_{j=i}^{S}\|\mathbf{z}_{j}-\mathbf{z}_{j-1}^{\star}\|.

Substituting this and changing the order of summations give

∑i=1S−1μi​‖𝐳S−𝐳i‖\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{S-1}\mu_{i}\|\mathbf{z}_{S}-\mathbf{z}_{i}\| ≤∑i=1S−1μi​∑j=iS‖𝐳j−𝐳j−1⋆‖\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{S-1}\mu_{i}\sum_{j=i}^{S}\|\mathbf{z}_{j}-\mathbf{z}_{j-1}^{\star}\|
=∑j=1S−1∑i=1jμi​‖𝐳j−𝐳j−1⋆‖+∑i=1S−1μi​‖𝐳S−𝐳S−1⋆‖.\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{S-1}\sum_{i=1}^{j}\mu_{i}\|\mathbf{z}_{j}-\mathbf{z}_{j-1}^{\star}\|+\sum_{i=1}^{S-1}\mu_{i}\|\mathbf{z}_{S}-\mathbf{z}_{S-1}^{\star}\|.

By using the setting μi=2i​μ\mu_{i}=2^{i}\mu, we have ∑i=1jμi=∑i=1j2i​μ≤2j+1​μ=μj+1=2​μj\sum_{i=1}^{j}\mu_{i}=\sum_{i=1}^{j}2^{i}\mu\leq 2^{j+1}\mu=\mu_{j+1}=2\mu_{j} and ∑i=1S−1μi≤μS\sum_{i=1}^{S-1}\mu_{i}\leq\mu_{S}, we get

∑i=1S−1μi​‖𝐳S−𝐳i‖\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{S-1}\mu_{i}\|\mathbf{z}_{S}-\mathbf{z}_{i}\| ≤2​∑j=1Sμj​‖𝐳j−𝐳j−1⋆‖.\displaystyle\leq 2\sum_{j=1}^{S}\mu_{j}\|\mathbf{z}_{j}-\mathbf{z}_{j-1}^{\star}\|.

Using this in (6.4) gives

‖𝒢η,Hμ​(𝐳S)‖≤‖𝒢η,HS−1​(𝐳S)‖+2​∑j=0S−1μj+1​‖𝐳j+1−𝐳j⋆‖,\displaystyle\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H^{\mu}}(\mathbf{z}_{S})\|\leq\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H^{S-1}}(\mathbf{z}_{S})\|+2\sum_{j=0}^{S-1}\mu_{j+1}\|\mathbf{z}_{j+1}-\mathbf{z}_{j}^{\star}\|, (6.5)

where we used the triangle inequality on the left-hand side of (6.4).

Next, we estimate ‖𝒢η,HS−1​(𝐳S)‖\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H^{S-1}}(\mathbf{z}_{S})\|. First, by the definition of 𝐳S−1⋆\mathbf{z}_{S-1}^{\star} (see (6.1)), we have

𝒢η,HS−1​(𝐳S−1⋆)=0\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H^{S-1}}(\mathbf{z}_{S-1}^{\star})=0 ⇔𝐳S−1⋆=proxη​r⁡(𝐳S−1⋆−η​FS−1​(𝐳S−1⋆))\displaystyle\iff\mathbf{z}_{S-1}^{\star}=\prox_{\eta r}(\mathbf{z}_{S-1}^{\star}-\eta F^{S-1}(\mathbf{z}_{S-1}^{\star}))
⇔𝐳S−1⋆+η​∂r⁡(𝐳S−1⋆)∋𝐳S−1⋆−η​FS−1​(𝐳S−1⋆)\displaystyle\iff\mathbf{z}_{S-1}^{\star}+\eta\partial r(\mathbf{z}_{S-1}^{\star})\ni\mathbf{z}_{S-1}^{\star}-\eta F^{S-1}(\mathbf{z}_{S-1}^{\star})
⇔0∈(∂r+FS−1)​(𝐳S−1⋆).\displaystyle\iff 0\in(\partial r+F^{S-1})(\mathbf{z}_{S-1}^{\star}).

Using this, we estimate as

‖𝒢η,HS−1​(𝐳S)‖\displaystyle\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H^{S-1}}(\mathbf{z}_{S})\| =‖𝒢η,HS−1​(𝐳S)−𝒢η,HS−1​(𝐳S−1⋆)‖\displaystyle=\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H^{S-1}}(\mathbf{z}_{S})-\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H^{S-1}}(\mathbf{z}_{S-1}^{\star})\|
≤η−1​(‖𝐳S−𝐳S−1⋆‖+‖proxη​r⁡(𝐳S−η​FS−1​(𝐳S))−proxη​r⁡(𝐳S−1⋆−η​FS−1​(𝐳S−1⋆))‖)\displaystyle\leq\eta^{-1}\left(\|\mathbf{z}_{S}-\mathbf{z}_{S-1}^{\star}\|+\|\prox_{\eta r}(\mathbf{z}_{S}-\eta F^{S-1}(\mathbf{z}_{S}))-\prox_{\eta r}(\mathbf{z}_{S-1}^{\star}-\eta F^{S-1}(\mathbf{z}_{S-1}^{\star}))\|\right)
≤η−1​(2​‖𝐳S−𝐳S−1⋆‖+η​‖FS−1​(𝐳S)−FS−1​(𝐳S−1⋆)‖)\displaystyle\leq\eta^{-1}\left(2\|\mathbf{z}_{S}-\mathbf{z}_{S-1}^{\star}\|+\eta\|F^{S-1}(\mathbf{z}_{S})-F^{S-1}(\mathbf{z}_{S-1}^{\star})\|\right)
≤η−1​(2​‖𝐳S−𝐳S−1⋆‖+η​LS−1​‖𝐳S−𝐳S−1⋆‖),\displaystyle\leq\eta^{-1}\left(2\|\mathbf{z}_{S}-\mathbf{z}_{S-1}^{\star}\|+\eta L_{S-1}\|\mathbf{z}_{S}-\mathbf{z}_{S-1}^{\star}\|\right),

where the first step is by triangle inequality, the second by triangle inequality and nonexpansiveness of the proximal operator, the third by the LS−1L_{S-1}-Lipschitzness of FS−1F^{S-1}. Since LS−1≤2​L^FL_{S-1}\leq 2\widehat{L}_{F}, we insert this into (6.5) to obtain the bound. ∎

This lemma is extending (CL, 24, Lemma 3.1) to using gradient mapping instead of the gradient and the existence of the regularizer rr in the subproblems. In contrast to (AZ, 18, Lemma 5.1), we cannot rely on inequalities specific to minimization such as the descent lemma.

Lemma 6.3.

Let FF be monotone and Fμ,(𝐳s⋆),(𝐳s)F^{\mu},(\mathbf{z}_{s}^{\star}),(\mathbf{z}_{s}) defined as (2.2), (2.3), and Algorithm 3, respectively. Set η=13​L^F\eta=\frac{1}{3\widehat{L}_{F}} where L^F=LF+B\widehat{L}_{F}=L_{F}+B. Then, we have

‖𝒢η,H​(𝐳S)‖≤2.5​∑j=1Sμj​‖𝐳j−𝐳j−1⋆‖+9​L^F​‖𝐳S−𝐳S−1⋆‖+μ​‖𝐳̊−𝐱⋆‖.\displaystyle\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H}(\mathbf{z}_{S})\|\leq 2.5\sum_{j=1}^{S}\mu_{j}\|\mathbf{z}_{j}-\mathbf{z}_{j-1}^{\star}\|+9\widehat{L}_{F}\|\mathbf{z}_{S}-\mathbf{z}_{S-1}^{\star}\|+\mu\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{x}^{\star}\|. (6.6)
Proof.

Since FF is only monotone, we are in the second case of (2.2). First, we characterize the difference between the residual for solving the original problem (MI) and the perturbed problem (2.1).

By the definition of the residual, we have

𝒢η,H​(𝐳)=η−1​(𝐳−proxη​r⁡(𝐳−η​F​(𝐳)))​ and ​𝒢η,Hμ​(𝐳)=η−1​(𝐳−proxη​r⁡(𝐳−η​Fμ​(𝐳))).\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H}(\mathbf{z})=\eta^{-1}\left(\mathbf{z}-\prox_{\eta r}(\mathbf{z}-\eta F(\mathbf{z}))\right)\text{~~~and~~~}\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H^{\mu}}(\mathbf{z})=\eta^{-1}\left(\mathbf{z}-\prox_{\eta r}(\mathbf{z}-\eta F^{\mu}(\mathbf{z}))\right).

With this, nonexpansiveness of the proximal operator and the triangle inequality, we obtain

‖𝒢η,H​(𝐳S)−𝒢η,Hμ​(𝐳S)‖≤‖F⁡(𝐳S)−Fμ​(𝐳S)‖≤μ|𝐳S−𝐳̊|≤μ⁡(‖𝐳S−𝐳0⋆‖+‖𝐳0⋆−𝐳̊‖),\displaystyle\|\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H}(\mathbf{z}_{S})-\mathcal{G}_{\eta,H^{\mu}}(\mathbf{z}_{S})\|\leq\|F(\mathbf{z}_{S})-F^{\mu}(\mathbf{z}_{S})\|\leq\mu\|\mathbf{z}_{S}-\mathring{\mathbf{z}}\|\leq\mu(\|\mathbf{z}_{S}-\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}\|+\|\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star}-\mathring{\mathbf{z}}\|), (6.7)

where 𝐳0⋆\mathbf{z}_{0}^{\star} is the solution of the perturbed problem as in (2.1) and the second inequality uses the definition in the second case of (2.2). For the second term on the right-hand side of (6.7), we can use Lemma 6.1 to get

‖𝐳̊−𝐳0⋆‖≤‖𝐳̊−𝐱⋆‖.\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{0}\|\leq\|\mathring{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{x}^{\star}\|. (6.8)

For the first term on the right-hand side of (6.7), we estimate similar to the proof of the Lemma 6.2:

Fact 6.5.

For getting precise constants for the complexity results and the parameters (see for example Section 4.2), we often solve inequalities of the form ex≥C​xe^{x}\geq Cx. ∎

7 Conclusions

Our goal in this work was to obtain a complexity result for the gradient mapping that is optimal up to logarithmic terms for solving constrained convex-concave min-max problems or stochastic VIs.

Our construction relied on the idea of recursive regularization of AZ (18) to get the best complexity, resulting in a three-loop construction. A clear direction for future research is to obtain the same complexity with a simpler approach, ideally with a single-loop algorithm. We believe that one may be able to go for a two-loop construction by combining KLL (22) and AZ (18), although it is not clear to us if this construction would still be able to handle the BG assumption. Obtaining the same complexity with a single-loop algorithm is open to our knowledge, even for minimization problems.

The second direction is analyzing the monotone case directly, rather than using perturbation by a small parameter μ\mu. This is necessary even for minimization problems to obtain the best gradient-norm guarantee to our knowledge, so we believe it is a question with a wider scope than min-max problems. Third, we believe that extension of our results to general monotone inclusions is possible by changing the inner solver. Finally, by using similar ideas to CL (24), we suspect it would be possible to allow some form of nonmonotonicity, to solve problems with cohypomonotone operators and constraints.
